extraction.name: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context (MS COCO)
extraction.description: A large-scale dataset for object detection and segmentation containing 2.5 million labeled instances in 328k images of complex everyday scenes. Objects are labeled using per-instance segmentations. The dataset contains 91 object categories and emphasizes non-iconic images with rich contextual relationships between objects.
extraction.creator: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollar
extraction.citeAs: T.-Y. Lin et al., 'Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context,' arXiv:1405.0312v3 [cs.CV], 21 Feb 2015.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Images were collected from Flickr using pairwise object category queries and scene-object category pairs to obtain non-iconic images. Workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk were used for annotation through a multi-stage pipeline including category labeling, instance spotting, and instance segmentation.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: 11 categories were excluded from the 2014 release due to issues such as too many instances, ambiguity, difficulty in labeling, confusion with other categories, or too few instances.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images collected from Flickr using pairwise object category queries and scene-object category pairs.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: First half released in 2014, second half to be released in 2015.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Near-duplicate images were explicitly removed and images were grouped by photographer and date taken to minimize duplicates across splits. An AMT filtering task was used to remove invalid or iconic images from candidate sets.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: A three-stage pipeline: (1) Category labeling using a hierarchical approach with 8 AMT workers per image to identify which object categories are present; (2) Instance spotting where 8 workers per image place crosses on all instances of each category; (3) Instance segmentation where a single worker segments each instance after passing a training task, followed by verification by 3-5 workers.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Worker precision and recall were analyzed by comparing AMT workers to expert annotators (co-authors). The union of 8 AMT workers achieved greater recall than any individual expert. Workers below a precision threshold were rejected. Segmentations not receiving at least 4 of 5 favorable votes were discarded.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 8 workers per image for category labeling and instance spotting; 1 worker per instance for segmentation; 3-5 workers for segmentation verification.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is split into two halves: first half released in 2014, second half to be released in 2015. MS COCO will evolve and grow over time.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset may contain biases due to the use of Flickr as an image source and the selection of object categories. The category selection process involved voting by co-authors and may reflect their perspectives. The dataset focuses on 'thing' categories and excludes 'stuff' categories.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset only includes 'thing' categories and not 'stuff' categories. 11 categories were excluded from the 2014 release. Dense crowds of objects are labeled as 'crowds' rather than individual instances. The dataset is limited to entry-level categories.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing for object detection and instance segmentation. The dataset is split into train, validation, and test sets. Annotations for train and validation data are released; test annotations are withheld for evaluation server use.

name.evidence: The Microsoft Common Objects in COntext (MS COCO) dataset contains 91 common object categories with 82 of them having more than 5,000 labeled instances

description.evidence: We present a new dataset with the goal of advancing the state-of-the-art in object recognition by placing the question of object recognition in the context of the broader question of scene understanding... With a total of 2.5 million labeled instances in 328k images

url.evidence: To download and learn more about MS COCO please see the project website. http://mscoco.org/

creator.evidence: Tsung-Yi Lin Michael Maire Serge Belongie Lubomir Bourdev Ross Girshick James Hays Pietro Perona Deva Ramanan C. Lawrence Zitnick Piotr Dollar

rai:dataCollection.evidence: We collected non-iconic images using two strategies. First as popularized by PASCAL VOC, we collected images from Flickr which tends to have fewer iconic images... For all crowdsourcing tasks we used workers on Amazon's Mechanical Turk (AMT).

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: We collected non-iconic images using two strategies. First as popularized by PASCAL VOC, we collected images from Flickr which tends to have fewer iconic images. Flickr contains photos uploaded by amateur photographers with searchable metadata and keywords. Second, we did not search for object categories in isolation... if we searched for pairwise combinations of object categories, such as 'dog + car' we found many more non-iconic images.

rai:dataCollectionMissingData.evidence: We have limited the 2014 release to a subset of 80 categories. We did not collect segmentations for the following 11 categories: hat, shoe, eyeglasses (too many instances), mirror, window, door, street sign (ambiguous and difficult to label), plate, desk (due to confusion with bowl and dining table, respectively) and blender, hair brush (too few instances).

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: We collected non-iconic images using two strategies. First as popularized by PASCAL VOC, we collected images from Flickr which tends to have fewer iconic images. Flickr contains photos uploaded by amateur photographers with searchable metadata and keywords.

rai:dataCollectionTimeframe.evidence: The first half of the dataset was released in 2014, the second half will be released in 2015.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: We took care to minimize the chance of near-duplicate images existing across splits by explicitly removing near duplicates (detected with [43]) and grouping images by photographer and date taken. We then created an AMT filtering task that allowed users to remove invalid or iconic images from a grid of 128 candidates.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: The annotation pipeline is outlined in Fig. 3. For all crowdsourcing tasks we used workers on Amazon's Mechanical Turk (AMT)... we have increased the number of annotators for the category labeling and instance spotting stages to eight. We also added a stage to verify the instance segmentations.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: For all crowdsourcing tasks we used workers on Amazon's Mechanical Turk (AMT).

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: Fig. 4(a) shows that the union of 8 AMT workers, the same number as was used to collect our labels, achieved greater recall than any of the expert workers... any segmentation that doesn't receive at least 4 of 5 favorable votes is discarded and the corresponding instance added back to the pool of unsegmented objects.

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: To ensure high recall, 8 workers were asked to label each image... Each image was labeled by 8 workers for a total of 10k worker hours... we only had a single worker segment each instance... Multiple workers (3 to 5) were asked to judge each segmentation.

rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan.evidence: To accommodate a faster release schedule, we split the MS COCO dataset into two roughly equal parts. The first half of the dataset was released in 2014, the second half will be released in 2015... MS COCO will evolve and grow over time; up to date information is available online.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: The selection of object categories is a non-trivial exercise. The categories must form a representative set of all categories, be relevant to practical applications and occur with high enough frequency to enable the collection of a large dataset... the co-authors voted on a 1 to 5 scale for each category taking into account how commonly they occur, their usefulness for practical applications, and their diversity relative to other categories.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: Since we are primarily interested in precise localization of object instances, we decided to only include 'thing' categories and not 'stuff.'... We have limited the 2014 release to a subset of 80 categories... After 10-15 instances of a category were segmented in an image, the remaining instances were marked as 'crowds' using a single (possibly multi-part) segment.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: The 2014 release contains 82,783 training, 40,504 validation, and 40,775 testing images... Following established protocol, annotations for train and validation data will be released, but not for test. We are currently finalizing the evaluation server for automatic evaluation on the test set.
